a: Herod the tetrarch
p: Not Herod the Great of chapter 2, but his son Antipas, who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39.
b: Herod the Great (2:1–22) died in 4 BC, and Rome split his kingdom among his sons. Herod Antipas got Galilee, where Jesus worked, and Perea, east of the Jordan, where John baptized. His title was tetrarch, "ruler of a quarter," a step below king. Matthew uses the correct title here, where Mark 6:14 says "King Herod," yet in 14:9 he slips into the popular "the king." Antipas built Tiberias as his capital on the lake. Jesus later called him "that fox" (Luke 13:32), and Luke has Pilate send Jesus to him at his trial (Luke 23:6–12). In AD 39 Antipas asked the emperor Caligula for the title of king and was exiled instead (Josephus, Antiquities 18.240–255).

a: He himself is raised from the dead.
p: Herod's fear tells us what people thought of Jesus. It is not a belief in reincarnation.
b: Herod's words have been read in several ways. A guilty conscience: the man who killed John cannot get him out of his mind (the view of most commentators since Chrysostom). Popular belief: some Jews expected great prophets to return (16:14; Malachi 4:5), and Herod voices the rumor that John has been raised to finish his work. It is not reincarnation, since Jesus and John were alive at the same time. Irony: John did no miracles (John 10:41), yet Herod thinks miraculous "powers" are now at work in him. Matthew's readers know the real answer: the one who will be raised from the dead is Jesus (16:21).

a: Herodias, who was the wife of Philip, Herod's brother
p: Josephus tells the same family story with one difference: he calls Herodias' first husband Herod, not Philip.
b: The Jewish historian Josephus (Antiquities 18.109–119, 136) says Antipas fell in love with Herodias, the wife of his half-brother, and divorced his first wife, a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV, to marry her. Herodias was also his niece. Josephus calls her first husband "Herod," a son of Herod the Great who lived as a private citizen, and says Philip the tetrarch married Herodias' daughter Salome. So either the first husband had two names ("Herod Philip" in later books), or the Gospel tradition confused two brothers. Aretas later went to war with Antipas over the insult and crushed his army in AD 36, and Josephus reports that many Jews saw the defeat as God's punishment for killing John.

a: The law does not allow you to have her.
t: "Not lawful": the Torah on a brother's wife
p: John was applying the law of Moses, which forbade marrying a brother's wife while the brother was alive.
b: "It is not lawful" (ouk exestin) is the language of Jewish legal debate: what the Torah allows. Leviticus says, "Do not expose the nakedness of your brother's wife" (Leviticus 18:16), and calls such a marriage "an unclean thing" (Leviticus 20:21). The one exception, levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10), applied only when the brother had died without a son. Herodias' husband was still alive. John was a prophet calling a Jewish ruler to the law he claimed to keep, like Nathan before David (2 Samuel 12) or Elijah before Ahab (1 Kings 21). That made it political: the ruler's marriage was publicly condemned by the most popular preacher in the land.
orig: Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν αὐτήν (ouk exestin soi echein autēn)

a: To them John was a prophet.
t: Why Antipas killed John: two accounts
p: Josephus says Antipas feared John might start a revolt. The Gospels give a personal reason. Both can be true.
b: Josephus (Antiquities 18.116–119) describes John as a good man who urged Jews to live justly and to come to baptism. Crowds gathered, and Antipas feared that John's power over the people might lead to an uprising, so he struck first, sent John in chains to the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and put him to death there. Matthew gives the personal and moral side: John condemned the marriage, and Herodias wanted revenge. Historians usually see the two accounts as fitting together. A prophet who publicly condemned the ruler's marriage was a political danger in a land where many already disliked the Herods.

a: the daughter of Herodias danced
p: The Gospels do not name her. Josephus says Herodias' daughter was Salome.
b: Matthew calls her only "the daughter of Herodias," and in 14:11 "the girl" (korasion, a word for a young girl, used of the twelve-year-old in 9:24–25). Josephus names Herodias' daughter Salome (Antiquities 18.136). A princess dancing for a ruler's male guests was shameful by the standards of the time, which is part of the point: the scene shows a court without restraint. Later art and literature, above all Oscar Wilde's play Salome (1891) and Richard Strauss's opera, invented the seductive "dance of the seven veils." The Gospels say nothing about the kind of dance.

a: This grieved the king.
p: Herod's oath recalls the Persian king in Esther, and Jephthah's terrible vow in Judges.
b: Mark 6:23 has Herod promise "Anything you ask me for, I will give you, even if it is half my kingdom," echoing the Persian king's words to Esther (Esther 5:3, 6; 7:2), and Matthew's shorter story still echoes that court scene. But here the queen asks for a prophet's death, not her people's life. A ruler trapped by a public oath also recalls Jephthah (Judges 11:30–39) and Saul (1 Samuel 14:24–45). Jesus warns against swearing oaths at all (5:33–37). Matthew calls Antipas "the king" here, the popular title, though Rome never granted it to him.
r: Esther 5:3; Esther 5:6; Esther 7:2; Judges 11:30–39; 1 Samuel 14:24–45; 5:33–37; Mark 6:23

a: Then they went to Jesus with the news.
p: Matthew links John's death to Jesus. The forerunner's fate shows what is coming for Jesus.
b: In Mark the story of John's death is a flashback. Matthew ties it into the plot: John's disciples bury him and go to tell Jesus, and Jesus then withdraws (14:13). Matthew often pairs the two men. Both preach "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near" (3:2; 4:17), both are seen as prophets (14:5; 21:11, 46), and both are arrested, killed by rulers who fear the crowd, and buried by disciples (27:57–60). Jesus says it outright in 17:12: as they did to John, "in the same way the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands."

a: went off alone to a lonely spot
p: Jesus often "withdraws" from danger in Matthew. The lonely place sets up a new wilderness meal.
b: "Left" here is anachōreō, "withdraw," a word Matthew uses when Jesus moves away from a threat: from Herod the Great (2:14, 22), after John's arrest (4:12), from the Pharisees' plot (12:15), and now after John's death. The "lonely spot" (erēmos topos) uses the word for wilderness. Israel was fed with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and the prophets promised a new exodus. The story that follows reads like God's people fed again in the wilderness by a greater Moses.

a: His heart went out to them
p: The Greek verb comes from the word for the inner organs. It is a gut-deep feeling, and it leads to action.
b: Splanchnizomai comes from splanchna, the inner organs, where people felt strong emotion. In the Gospels it describes Jesus (9:36; 14:14; 15:32; 20:34) and the master in the parable who forgives the huge debt (18:27). In Luke it describes the Samaritan and the father of the lost son (Luke 10:33; Luke 15:20). Each time, the feeling turns into action: healing, feeding, forgiving. Matthew presents it as God's own mercy at work, the shepherd's care of Ezekiel 34.

a: said the blessing
p: A Jewish meal began with a blessing of God. The verbs here return at the Last Supper.
b: Matthew says simply that Jesus "blessed" (eulogēsen), with no object. In Jewish practice the blessing before a meal praises God, not the food; the Mishnah gives the blessing over bread as "who brings forth bread from the earth" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:1). Looking up to heaven was a gesture of prayer. The four verbs, took, blessed, broke, gave, are the same verbs Matthew uses at the Last Supper (26:26). Many readers since the early church have seen the feeding as a picture of the Lord's Supper, though the meal here is bread and fish, not bread and wine.

a: Everyone ate until they were full.
p: The only miracle in all four Gospels: read as a miracle, a lesson in sharing, or a sign of the end-time feast.
b: A miracle of multiplication: the church's traditional reading, and the plain sense of the story: five loaves fed thousands, with more left over than at the start. A rational explanation: some 1800s scholars (H. E. G. Paulus) proposed that Jesus' example moved people to share food they had hidden; the text says nothing of this. A sign: many scholars stress what the story means. It echoes manna (Exodus 16), Elisha's feeding (2 Kings 4:42–44), and the promised banquet of the end time (Isaiah 25:6; 8:11). John 6:14–15 says the crowd wanted to make Jesus king afterward, a sign that people read it as a messianic act. Most historians accept that a remembered wilderness meal lies behind the story, whatever they think of the miracle.

a: twelve full baskets
p: More is left than was there at first. Twelve is Israel's number.
b: Elisha's servant fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, "and there was extra, just as the LORD's word had said" (2 Kings 4:44). Jesus feeds thousands with five, and twelve baskets are left. Twelve recalls the twelve tribes and the Twelve (10:1–4; 19:28), so many readers see Israel fed and restored here. The basket (kophinos) was a stiff wicker basket that the Roman poet Juvenal links with Jews (Satires 3.14), perhaps because travelers carried their own kosher food. Compare the seven big baskets of the second feeding (15:37; 16:9–10).

a: apart from women and children
p: Only Matthew mentions women and children. The crowd may have been far larger than five thousand.
b: Ancient counts often numbered only men, as in the exodus: "about six hundred thousand men on foot, not counting the little ones" (Exodus 12:37). Matthew alone adds "apart from women and children" here and at 15:38, perhaps to make the miracle greater, perhaps to remind readers that whole families followed Jesus. The note may also echo the exodus count and strengthen the picture of a new Israel in the wilderness.

a: he made the disciples get into the boat
p: The verb means "compelled." John's Gospel gives a reason: the crowd wanted to make Jesus king.
b: Ēnankasen means he "compelled" or "forced" them. Matthew does not say why Jesus was in such a hurry. John 6:14–15 says that after the feeding the people were about to take Jesus by force to make him king, so he withdrew to the mountain alone. If that is the background, Jesus separated the disciples from a crowd ready for a political Messiah, the kind of kingship he refuses in 4:8–10.

a: he climbed the mountain to pray in private
p: Matthew places key moments on a mountain, as with Moses at Sinai.
b: Mountains mark turning points in Matthew: the testing (4:8), the great sermon (5:1), healing and feeding (15:29), the transfiguration (17:1), and the last commission (28:16). Moses went up the mountain to meet God alone (Exodus 24:12–18; 34:2–3), and Elijah prayed on Carmel and met God on Horeb (1 Kings 18:42; 1 Kings 19:8–12). Jesus' night of prayer alone points ahead to Gethsemane (26:36–46).

a: walking on the sea
t: The one who walks on the sea
p: In the Old Testament only God walks on the sea and tames its waves.
b: To first readers the sea was the place of chaos, and power over it belonged to God. Job says God "tramples on the back of the Sea" (Job 9:8), and the psalm of the exodus says to God, "Your road was in the sea" (Psalm 77:19). God also asks Job, "Have you walked about where the deep is deepest?" (Job 38:16). God "opened a road in the sea" (Isaiah 43:16) and calms the storm (Psalm 107:29). When Jesus walks on the waters and later the wind stops (14:32), Matthew shows Jesus doing what Scripture says God does. The disciples' bowing down in 14:33 is the right response.

a: It's a phantom!
p: The word is phantasma, an apparition. Many people believed in night spirits, and the sea was their home.
b: Phantasma means something that appears, an apparition. Greek and Jewish folk belief knew of spirits that walked at night, and the sea was linked with demonic powers (8:28–32 ends with demons sent into the sea). The disciples' terror is real: a figure walking on the water at three in the morning could only be a spirit. Jesus' answer, "It is I," replaces the phantom with a person.

a: I am.
p: Jesus says "egō eimi," "I am." It means "It's me," but it can also echo God's name.
b: Egō eimi is ordinary Greek for "It's me." But in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, "LXX") God speaks the same words: "I am the one who is" (Exodus 3:14, LXX), "so that you may know and believe ... that I am" (Isaiah 43:10, LXX), and "I am, I am the one who comforts you" (Isaiah 51:12, LXX). Along with walking on the sea (14:25), many interpreters hear a hint of God's self-naming. Others think the words mean only "Don't fear, it's me, not a ghost." Matthew may intend both levels. "Do not be afraid" is also God's word to Israel in Isaiah 41:10, 13 and 43:1–5.
r: Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 41:10; Isaiah 43:1–5; Isaiah 43:10; Isaiah 51:12; Mark 6:50; John 6:20; John 8:58

a: Lord, if it is really you
t: Peter on the water: only in Matthew
p: Mark and John tell of Jesus on the sea. Only Matthew adds Peter's walk.
b: Matthew has several Peter stories found in no other Gospel: walking on the water (14:28–31), the blessing and the keys (16:17–19), the coin in the fish (17:24–27) and the question about forgiveness (18:21). They make Peter the leading disciple and a model of the believer: bold, sincere, sinking, and saved. Traditional readers take the scene as history and as a lesson in faith (Chrysostom). Critical scholars often think Matthew drew it from a local Peter tradition or shaped it as a picture of discipleship. Peter's "If it is you" recalls the devil's "If you are the Son of God" (4:3, 6), but Peter asks for a command, not a proof.

a: He started to go under
t: Claude's theory: the Rock that sank
p: Claude's reading: Matthew's Rock sinks like Pharaoh's army. The argument is in the box on the chapter page.
b: This is my own suggestion, not a standard reading. The verb for sinking here, katapontizomai, is the one the Greek of Exodus 15:4 uses for Pharaoh's officers sunk in the Red Sea, and it returns in Matthew only at 18:6. Two chapters later Simon is named the Rock (16:18). The full argument, and its limits, are in the box "Claude's theory: the Rock that sank" on the chapter 14 page.

a: Lord, save me!
p: Peter's cry is the cry of the drowning in the Psalms.
b: "Save me, God, for the water has reached my throat" (Psalm 69:1) is the prayer of one sinking "in the mud of the deep." The Psalms often picture God rescuing his servant from deep waters (Psalm 18:16; Psalm 144:7). "Lord, save" is also the disciples' cry in the earlier storm (8:25). For Matthew's readers, a church under pressure, Peter's three words became a model prayer.

a: You with so little faith
p: Matthew's special word: the disciples are not unbelievers, but their faith is too small.
b: Oligopistos, "of little faith," is almost Matthew's own word (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8; and the noun in 17:20; elsewhere only Luke 12:28). It never describes outsiders, only disciples who believe but falter. "Waver" (distazō) means to be of two minds; the only other New Testament use is 28:17, where some of the Eleven "wavered" even as they worshiped the risen Jesus. Matthew's picture of faith is honest: doubt and worship can live in the same person.
orig: Ὀλιγόπιστε, εἰς τί ἐδίστασας (oligopiste, eis ti edistasas)

a: You really are God's Son.
p: Mark ends this scene with the disciples' hardened hearts. Matthew ends it with bowing down and a confession.
b: In Mark 6:51–52 the disciples are amazed, "for their hearts were hardened." Matthew instead has them bow before Jesus and say, "Truly you are God's Son," which prepares for Peter's confession in 16:16. The verb proskyneō, "bow down," can mean bowing to a king or worshiping God, and the Plain English Translation keeps the bodily act; Matthew uses it often of people before Jesus (2:11; 8:2; 15:25; 28:9, 17). "Son of God" had several meanings for Jews: Israel (Exodus 4:22), the Davidic king (Psalm 2:7) or the righteous. Christian readers hear the full sense of 3:17 and 17:5. Historians debate how much the first disciples meant by it.

a: Gennesaret
p: A fertile plain on the northwest shore of the lake, between Capernaum and Magdala.
b: Gennesaret was a small, rich plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee; Josephus praises its climate and fruit (Jewish War 3.516–521), and Luke calls the lake itself "the lake of Gennesaret" (Luke 5:1). In 1986, during a drought, a fishing boat from about the time of Jesus was found in the mud near Ginosar on this shore: about 27 feet long and 7 feet wide, big enough for a crew of a dozen or so. It gives a good idea of the kind of boat in 14:22–33.

a: the tassel on his cloak
p: Jesus wore the tassels the law commands on the corners of a cloak. "Hem" and "edge" hide this.
b: Kraspedon is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tassels (Hebrew tsitsit) that Israelite men were to wear on the corners of their clothes: "Tell them to make tassels for themselves on the corners of their clothes" (Numbers 15:38). Matthew shows Jesus as an observant Jew who wore them (also 9:20), and he criticizes only those who make them long for show (23:5). The sick may have hoped that touching the sign of God's commands would bring God's power.
orig: τοῦ κρασπέδου τοῦ ἱματίου (tou kraspedou tou himatiou)

a: a group of Pharisees and scribes arrived from Jerusalem
p: Matthew presents an official-looking delegation. Its question is about purity, a live issue among Jews.
b: Jerusalem was the home of the Temple and of leading teachers, so visitors "from Jerusalem" carry weight (compare 3:7; Mark 3:22). The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to keeping the law carefully, including purity rules and traditions not written in the Torah. Scribes were experts in the law, some of them Pharisees. This is a debate among Jews about how to live God's law, and Jesus answers as a Jewish teacher, citing the Torah and the prophets. See the note at 3:7 on the Pharisees and Sadducees.

a: the tradition of the elders
p: The Pharisees' unwritten rules, handed down by teachers. Rabbinic Judaism later called this the Oral Torah.
b: Paradosis means what is handed down. Josephus says the Pharisees "passed on to the people certain rules handed down by the fathers, which are not written in the laws of Moses," and that the Sadducees rejected them (Antiquities 13.297). Later rabbis taught that Moses received an oral Torah at Sinai along with the written one and passed it down through the elders (Mishnah Avot 1:1). For the Pharisees these traditions were a "fence" to help people keep the commands. Jesus does not reject tradition as such here; he objects when a tradition sets aside a command of God (15:3–6). Christians later used this passage in their own debates over Scripture and church tradition (see the card on the chapter page).
orig: τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων (tēn paradosin tōn presbyterōn)

a: They do not wash their hands
p: This was about ritual purity, not hygiene. The Torah asked it only of priests.
b: The law of Moses required priests to wash their hands and feet before serving at the altar (Exodus 30:19–21). Some Pharisees sought to eat ordinary meals in the purity of priests, and hand-washing before bread became part of that. The Mishnah later gives a whole tractate to the purity of hands (Mishnah Yadayim), and the rite is still practiced in Jewish homes. How widely ordinary Jews kept it in Jesus' day is debated: E. P. Sanders argues it was a pious practice of a minority, not yet a general rule. The question is not germs, which no one knew of, but whether impurity on the hands passes into the food and so into the person.

a: 'Honor your father and mother,' and, 'Anyone who speaks evil of father or mother must be put to death.'
p: Jesus quotes the fifth commandment and the law that protected it.
b: The first quotation is the fifth of the Ten Words (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16). The second is Exodus 21:17 (also Leviticus 20:9). Matthew follows the Greek Old Testament, "speaks evil of" (kakologeō); the Hebrew has qillel, which the site renders "Anyone who curses his father or his mother must be put to death" (Exodus 21:17). The Hebrew word also means to treat as light or worthless, which fits Jesus' point well: a son who leaves his parents without support treats them as worthless. In Jewish teaching, honoring parents included feeding and caring for them in old age.

a: is an offering
t: Korban: a vow that hurt parents
p: Mark gives the Hebrew word, korban. A son could declare his property an offering and so out of his parents' reach.
b: Matthew's dōron, "gift, offering," stands for the Hebrew korban, as Mark 7:11 explains. Saying "Korban!" over something was a vow formula: it made the thing like an offering to the Temple, forbidden to the person named, even if it never reached the altar. A son could use it to cut his parents off from his help. An ossuary lid found near Jerusalem bears the word qrbn to keep grave robbers away, showing how the formula was used. Jesus says the vow cancels God's command. Later rabbis agreed: the Mishnah allows such a vow to be released when it harms one's father and mother (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1). So this is a dispute inside Judaism, and Jesus' side later won.

a: This people gives me honor with their lips
p: Jesus quotes Isaiah as it reads in the Greek Old Testament, which differs from the Hebrew in the second half.
b: In Isaiah 29:13 the Hebrew says the people's fear of God "is a command of men, learned by heart." The Greek translation reads, "In vain they worship me, teaching commands of men and teachings," and Matthew follows that wording closely (15:9). The Greek sharpens the point Jesus is making: worship becomes empty when human rules take the place of God's word. Isaiah spoke to Jerusalem in the late 700s BC, when its leaders trusted in their own plans. Paul quotes the following verse, Isaiah 29:14, in 1 Corinthians 1:19.

a: What enters a person's mouth does not make him unclean.
t: Did Jesus set aside the food laws?
p: Mark adds "declaring all foods clean." Matthew does not, and his story ends with washing hands.
b: Mark 7:19 adds a comment: "With this he made all foods clean." Matthew leaves it out and ends with "eating without washing your hands does not make anyone unclean" (15:20). Many scholars (Davies and Allison, Luz) conclude that Matthew's Jesus speaks about hand-washing and the purity of food, not about the kosher laws, which Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers may still have kept (5:17–19). Others say the principle (what defiles comes from the heart) undercuts the food laws, as Paul and Acts later concluded (Acts 10:9–16; Romans 14:14). Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes read it as a prophet's "not this, but that," like "Loyal love is what I want, not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6): a statement of priority, not abolition.

a: Any plant that was not planted by my heavenly Father
p: Israel was God's planting in the prophets. The Dead Sea community called itself an eternal planting.
b: The prophets picture God's people as a planting: "the shoot I planted" (Isaiah 60:21) and people called "Oaks of Righteousness," planted by the LORD (Isaiah 61:3). The community of the Dead Sea Scrolls called itself "an everlasting planting" (Community Rule, 1QS 8:5; compare Damascus Document 1:7). Jesus implies that the Pharisees' teaching is not part of God's planting and will not last. He also says "Let them be": the uprooting is God's work, as in the parable of the weeds (13:24–30, 40–43).

a: When one blind man leads another, both of them will fall into a ditch.
p: A proverb Jesus uses again in chapter 23. Jewish teachers saw themselves as guides of the blind.
b: Luke 6:39 has the same saying in a different setting. Matthew uses "blind guides" again in the woes of chapter 23 (23:16, 24). The image cuts deep because Jewish teachers saw guiding the blind as their calling: Paul describes a Jewish teacher as "a guide to the blind, a light to people in darkness" (Romans 2:19). The open pit or ditch was a real danger on dark country roads.

a: Tell us what this parable means.
p: Parabolē covers any saying with a hidden point: a riddle, a proverb, a picture.
b: Peter calls the one-line saying of 15:11 a parable. Parabolē translates Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs, riddles, taunts and stories. A saying that sounded like a riddle about food needed explaining, and Jesus does so privately for the disciples, as with the parables of chapter 13 (13:10–18, 36). Peter speaks for the group, as he often does in Matthew.

a: murders, adulteries, acts of sexual immorality, thefts, false testimony, slanders
t: The Ten Words, from the heart
p: Matthew orders this list like the second half of the Ten Commandments.
b: Mark 7:21–22 lists thirteen vices. Matthew has seven and puts them in the order of the commandments: murder, adultery, theft, false witness (Exodus 20:13–16), with "sexual immorality" (porneiai) beside adultery and "slanders" (blasphēmiai, abusive speech, against people or God) after false testimony. The point is the one Jesus made in 5:21–28: the commands are broken first in the heart, where "evil plans" begin.

a: the area around Tyre and Sidon
p: The old Phoenician port cities on the coast north of Galilee, Gentile territory.
b: Tyre and Sidon, on the coast of today's Lebanon, were ancient Phoenician cities, rich trading ports often condemned by the prophets (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28). In Jesus' day their territory bordered Galilee, and many Galileans traded with them. Jesus has already said that Tyre and Sidon would have repented if they had seen his miracles (11:21–22). Matthew is careful about whether Jesus entered Gentile land: the woman "came out" from those borderlands toward him, while Mark 7:24 says Jesus went into the region.

a: a Canaanite woman
p: Mark calls her a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth. Matthew uses the ancient name of Israel's enemies in the land.
b: No one in Jesus' day called themselves Canaanites in Greek; Mark 7:26 calls her "a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth." Matthew chooses the old biblical name. Sidon was "the firstborn of Canaan" (Genesis 10:15), and the Canaanites were the peoples Israel was told to drive out and not marry (Deuteronomy 7:1–3). The name raises the stakes: an outsider of the oldest kind comes asking for mercy. Yet Matthew's genealogy already includes Rahab, a Canaanite, and Tamar, probably one (1:3, 5), and the outcome here reverses the old hostility.

a: Lord, Son of David
p: The woman uses the royal title for the Messiah. The irony is sharp: the outsider sees what the leaders miss.
b: "Son of David" is a title of the Messiah in Matthew (1:1; 9:27; 12:23; 20:30–31; 21:9, 15). It is usually the needy and the outsiders who use it: blind men, the crowds, children in the Temple. Here a Gentile woman addresses Jesus as Israel's king, while the teachers from Jerusalem argue with him about hand-washing. Solomon, the first "son of David," was known in Jewish tradition as a healer and exorcist, which may also lie behind the title in healing stories.

a: Send her off.
t: "Send her off": rid of her, or help her?
p: The disciples may mean "get rid of her" or "give her what she wants and let her go."
b: Apolyson means "release, dismiss." The disciples may want Jesus to drive her away, or to grant her request so she will stop shouting. Jesus' answer in 15:24 explains why he will not grant it, which suggests the second meaning. Either way the disciples care more about their peace than about her daughter.

a: the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost
p: Jesus' mission is to Israel first. After Easter the disciples are sent to all nations.
b: Jesus told the Twelve to stay off the roads to the Gentiles and go instead "to the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost" (10:5–6). The phrase echoes the prophets, who called Israel lost sheep scattered by bad shepherds (Jeremiah 50:6; Ezekiel 34:4–16). Readers have explained the limit in several ways. Salvation history: Israel first, then the nations (28:19; Romans 1:16; Romans 15:8). Historical: the historical Jesus worked among Jews, and the Gentile mission came later. Jewish reading: scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine stress that Matthew's Jesus is a Jew sent to renew Israel, not to found a new religion. The woman's faith shows that the blessing for Israel overflows to the nations, as the prophets foresaw (Isaiah 56:6–8).

a: the little dogs
p: Jesus compares Gentiles to dogs. Readers have long struggled with the words.
b: "Dogs" was an insult, and Jews sometimes used it of Gentiles; Paul turns it on his opponents (Philippians 3:2). The word here is kynaria, "little dogs," household pets rather than street dogs, which softens it a little but does not remove the sting. Readings: A test of faith: Jesus intended to help and drew out her faith (Chrysostom, Calvin). Jesus changed: many modern scholars think Jesus was genuinely moved by her answer and widened his mission (a reading developed by feminist interpreters). Priority, not contempt: the saying is a proverb about order, children fed first (Mark 7:27 adds "first"). Whatever the intent, the woman wins the argument, and Jesus praises her as no one else in Matthew.

a: your faith is great!
p: In Matthew only two people are praised for great faith, and both are Gentiles.
b: The Roman centurion (8:5–13) and this Canaanite woman are the only people in Matthew whose faith Jesus praises as great. In both stories Jesus heals at a distance, and the healing comes "from that hour" (8:13; 15:28). Both contrast with the disciples' "little faith" (14:31; 16:8) and with Israel's leaders. Matthew's readers, who were learning to welcome Gentiles (28:19), saw in them the first fruits of the nations.

a: they gave glory to the God of Israel
p: "The God of Israel" may hint that the healed were Gentiles. Scholars disagree.
b: Mark 7:31 places the healing in the Decapolis, the mostly Gentile cities east of the lake. Matthew gives no place but says the crowd praised "the God of Israel," a phrase a Gentile crowd might use. Some scholars (Gundry, Keener) read the healings and the second feeding as Jesus' ministry to Gentiles, following the Canaanite woman. Others (Davies and Allison) note that Jews also praised "the God of Israel" (Psalm 41:13; Luke 1:68) and that Matthew says nothing of a Gentile crowd. The list of healings fulfills Isaiah 35:5–6, as in Jesus' answer to John (11:5).

a: My heart goes out to this crowd
p: The second feeding is close to the first. Some think it is the same event told twice.
b: Matthew and Mark both tell two feedings (14:13–21; 15:32–39; Mark 6:30–44; Mark 8:1–10), and Jesus refers to both (16:9–10). Many critical scholars think the tradition told one event in two versions, since the disciples' question in 15:33 is odd if they had just seen the first. Traditional readers take them as two events, as the text presents them (Augustine, Harmony of the Gospels 2.50). Symbolic readings by some church fathers and later writers take the first feeding as Israel's (twelve baskets, twelve tribes) and the second as the Gentiles' (seven, the number of completeness). Matthew's own point is the repetition: the disciples keep forgetting (16:8–11).

a: the district of Magadan
p: No one knows. It may be another name for Magdala, as later copyists thought.
b: Magadan is not mentioned anywhere else, and its location is unknown. Mark's parallel has "Dalmanutha" (Mark 8:10), also unknown. Many guess Magdala, home of Mary Magdalene, on the west shore, where a first-century synagogue was found in 2009. Other suggestions place it on the east side of the lake. See the variant on this verse.

a: Pharisees and Sadducees
p: The two groups disagreed sharply, yet Matthew shows them testing Jesus together.
b: The Sadducees were a party of priestly and wealthy families centered on the Temple. They accepted only the written law, denied the resurrection (22:23; Acts 23:8) and rejected the Pharisees' traditions. Matthew pairs the two groups here and in 3:7 and 16:6–12 as a united front of Israel's leaders. Historians note that Sadducees were rarely seen in Galilee and that Mark 8:11 names only Pharisees. Many think Matthew, writing after the Temple fell in AD 70, when the Sadducees disappeared, groups the old leaders together. Others think the alliance of powerful opponents is historical.

a: They wanted to put him to the test
t: Testing Jesus as the devil did
p: "Test" is the verb used of the devil in the wilderness. Demanding a sign from heaven repeats Israel's testing of God.
b: Peirazō, "test, tempt," is the verb used of the devil, "the tester" (4:1, 3). The leaders now play the tester's role, as they will again (19:3; 22:18, 35). A "sign out of heaven" would be proof straight from God, like manna or Elijah's fire. Jesus already answered the devil from Deuteronomy: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16). He refuses to perform on demand here too.

a: The signs of the times
p: Not the weather, but what God is doing now in Jesus and John.
b: Kairoi, "times," are moments of opportunity, God's appointed seasons. The signs are already present: the blind see and the lame walk (11:5; 15:30–31), the kingdom is breaking in (12:28). People who read the sky every day cannot read God's work in front of them. Today the phrase is often used for end-time events; in Matthew it is about the present moment of Jesus' ministry. On whether these words belong in Matthew at all, see the variant on 16:2–3.
orig: τὰ σημεῖα τῶν καιρῶν (ta sēmeia tōn kairōn)

a: A generation that is evil and adulterous
p: "Adulterous" is the prophets' word for Israel's unfaithfulness to God, not only sexual sin.
b: The prophets pictured God as Israel's husband and idolatry as adultery (Hosea 2:2–13; Jeremiah 3:6–10; Ezekiel 16). Moses' song calls Israel "a warped and twisted generation" (Deuteronomy 32:5). Jesus says the same words here as in 12:39, where he explains "the sign of Jonah": as Jonah was three days in the fish, the Son of Man will be three days in the earth (12:40), and Nineveh's repentance will judge this generation (12:41).

a: the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees
p: Yeast, or sourdough starter, spreads through a whole batch. Matthew explains it as their teaching.
b: Ancient bakers kept back a lump of fermented dough (leaven) to start the next batch. A little spreads through the whole, so yeast became a picture of an influence, usually a bad one: Israel removed all leaven at Passover (Exodus 12:15–20), and Paul says "a little yeast leavens the whole batch" (1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9). Jesus uses it once in a good sense, for the kingdom (13:33). Matthew explains this yeast as the "teaching" of the two groups (16:12); Luke 12:1 calls it hypocrisy, and Mark 8:15 speaks of the yeast of Herod. Since the Pharisees and Sadducees taught very different things, Matthew probably means a shared attitude, perhaps their demand for signs and their refusal to believe, more than shared doctrines. Compare 23:2–3, where Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees say.

a: Have you forgotten the five loaves and the five thousand
p: Jesus asks the disciples to remember, as Moses asked Israel to remember the manna.
b: "Remember" is Deuteronomy's word: remember how God fed you with manna in the wilderness, so that you would know that people do not live on bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:2–3), the verse Jesus quoted when he was tested (4:4). The disciples worry about bread on the day after two feedings. Matthew softens Mark's harsher scene (Mark 8:17–21, "Are your hearts hardened?"), and his disciples finally understand (16:12).

a: Caesarea Philippi
p: A city at the foot of Mount Hermon, by a spring of the Jordan, full of pagan shrines.
b: Caesarea Philippi stood about 25 miles north of the Sea of Galilee, at a spring that feeds the Jordan, below Mount Hermon. Its older name was Panias, for a cave shrine of the Greek god Pan, which still gives the site its modern name, Banias. Herod the Great built a temple to Augustus there, and his son Philip the tetrarch rebuilt the town and named it Caesarea for the emperor, "Philip's" to tell it from Caesarea on the coast. Jesus asks his question at the edge of the Jewish world, among shrines to Pan and to Caesar. Some preachers link the great rock face and the cave, thought to lead to the underworld, to "this rock" and "the gates of Hades" (16:18); that is an attractive idea, but the text does not say it.

a: the Son of Man
p: Jesus' favorite name for himself. It can mean simply "a human being," and it echoes Daniel 7.
b: In Hebrew and Aramaic "son of man" means a human being (Psalm 8:4; Ezekiel 2:1). In Daniel 7:13 "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds and receives a kingdom. Jesus uses the phrase of himself about 30 times in Matthew, for his humble life (8:20), his coming suffering (17:22) and his coming glory (16:27; 24:30; 26:64). Scholars debate how the first hearers took it: as a plain "I" or "a man like me" (Geza Vermes), as Daniel's heavenly figure, or as an open title that Jesus filled with his own meaning. Here Matthew puts it in the question itself; in Mark 8:27 Jesus asks, "Who do people say I am?"
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

a: Still others say Jeremiah
p: Only Matthew adds Jeremiah to the list. He was the prophet who suffered and wept over Jerusalem.
b: Matthew alone names Jeremiah, here and as the source of two fulfillment quotations (2:17; 27:9). Jeremiah was rejected, beaten and imprisoned, and he warned that the Temple would be destroyed (Jeremiah 7; 26), much as Jesus does (24:2). In 2 Maccabees 15:13–16 Jeremiah appears in a dream as a heavenly intercessor for Israel, so some Jews expected him to return. Elijah's return was promised in Malachi 4:5. People take Jesus for a prophet like these, which is true but not enough.

a: You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.
p: Mark has "You are the Messiah." Matthew adds "the Son of the living God."
b: Peter's answer gives Jesus the two titles that frame Matthew's story: "the Messiah," Israel's anointed king of David's line (1:1, 16–18), and "the Son of God" (3:17; 14:33; 26:63; 27:54). "The living God" is an Old Testament title that sets Israel's God against lifeless idols (Deuteronomy 5:26; Psalm 42:2; Hosea 1:10). Mark 8:29 has only "You are the Messiah," and Luke 9:20 "God's Messiah." For historians, Peter's words in Jesus' lifetime probably meant Israel's promised king. Christian tradition has heard in Matthew's fuller words the confession of the church's creeds. Jesus calls the insight a gift from the Father (16:17).

a: Simon Bar-Jonah
p: Bar is Aramaic for "son." John's Gospel calls Peter's father John, perhaps the same name.
b: Bariōna is Aramaic: "son of Jonah." John's Gospel calls Simon "son of John" (John 1:42; John 21:15–17). Jonah may be a short form of Yohanan (John), or Peter's father may have had two names. Some readers see a link with "the sign of Jonah" just mentioned (16:4). Using his full name, Jesus speaks formally, as if conferring a new name and office: Simon son of Jonah becomes Peter. "Flesh and blood" is a Jewish way of saying "human beings" (Galatians 1:16; Sirach 14:18).

a: you are Peter, and on this rock
p: Petros and petra are both "rock." In Aramaic both would be Kepha. What is the rock?
b: Jesus puns on Simon's new name: Petros (Peter) and petra (rock). In Aramaic both would be Kepha, the "Cephas" of John 1:42 and Paul's letters. In older Greek petros was a stone and petra a mass of rock. Most scholars today think the difference matters little here: the words had largely merged by this period, and a man's name needed the masculine form. Some, such as Chrys Caragounis, still argue that the change of word points away from Peter to his confession. What is the rock? Peter himself, as leader of the apostles: the plainest reading of the pun, held by Catholic teaching and by many Protestant scholars (Oscar Cullmann, R. T. France). Peter's confession of faith: Chrysostom often, Luther and many Protestant and Orthodox readers. Christ himself, the rock (1 Corinthians 3:11; 1 Corinthians 10:4): a reading Augustine came to prefer while leaving the choice to the reader (Retractations 1.21). Every believer who confesses like Peter: Origen. Whether the promise passes to Peter's successors is a separate question (see the card on the chapter page).
r: John 1:42; 1 Corinthians 15:5; Galatians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 3:11; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Isaiah 51:1–2; 7:24–25
orig: σὺ εἶ Πέτρος, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ (sy ei Petros, kai epi tautē tē petra)

a: I will build my church
p: One of only two places the Gospels use the word. In the Greek Old Testament it means the assembly of Israel.
b: Ekklēsia means an assembly, people called out and gathered. The Greek Old Testament uses it for qahal, the assembly of Israel gathered before God, as on "the day of the assembly" at Sinai (Deuteronomy 9:10; Deuteronomy 18:16). The Gospels use the word only here and in 18:17. "My" church means a community that belongs to Jesus and is built by him, as God builds his people (Jeremiah 24:6; Amos 9:11). Many critical scholars think the wording reflects the later church, since Jesus rarely speaks of a community after his death. Others reply that a Messiah gathering a renewed Israel, with an Aramaic word such as qehala, fits Jesus well. The War Scroll from Qumran writes "the assembly of God" on the banners of its end-time army (1QM 4:10).
r: 18:17; Deuteronomy 9:10; Deuteronomy 18:16; Jeremiah 24:6; Amos 9:11; Acts 7:38; Ephesians 2:19–22
orig: οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν (oikodomēsō mou tēn ekklēsian)

a: the gates of Hades will not be stronger than it
p: Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the place of the dead. Its gates will not hold the church.
b: Hades is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Sheol, the world of the dead. "The gates of Sheol" or "the gates of death" were a common image: "Has anyone opened death's gates to you?" (Job 38:17; also Psalm 9:13; Psalm 107:18; Isaiah 38:10). Readings: Death will not win: the church, and its members, will not be held by death, because its Lord will rise (the most common modern reading). The powers of evil will not overcome it. The church on the attack: gates do not move, so the church will storm death's gates and free its prisoners; some fathers linked this to Christ's descent to the dead (1 Peter 3:19). The KJV's "gates of hell" can mislead: the word is not Gehenna.
r: Job 38:17; Psalm 9:13; Psalm 107:18; Isaiah 38:10; Revelation 1:18; 1 Peter 3:19; 1 Corinthians 15:54–55
orig: πύλαι ᾅδου οὐ κατισχύσουσιν αὐτῆς (pylai hadou ou katischysousin autēs)

a: To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.
p: Keys mark the steward of a royal house. Isaiah 22 gives Eliakim "the key of the house of David."
b: In Isaiah 22:20–22 God gives the steward Eliakim "the key of the house of David": what he opens no one shuts, and what he shuts no one opens. The palace steward held the king's authority over the household. Revelation 3:7 applies that key to Christ. Jesus later accuses the scribes and Pharisees of shutting the kingdom in people's faces (23:13; compare Luke 11:52, "the key of knowledge"). Peter's keys, then, are a steward's authority: to open the kingdom by teaching and admitting people. Catholic teaching sees here a lasting office; Protestant readers usually see Peter's role in preaching the first gospel to Jews and Gentiles (Acts 2; Acts 10).

a: Anything you bind on earth will stand bound in heaven
p: A Jewish teachers' phrase for forbidding and allowing, and also for putting out and taking back.
b: "Bind" and "loose" were technical terms among Jewish teachers: to bind was to forbid, to loose to permit. Josephus says that under Queen Alexandra the Pharisees had power "to loose and to bind" (Jewish War 1.111). The pair can also mean putting someone under a ban and lifting it, the sense in 18:17–18. The Greek is a future with a perfect participle, "will be having been bound." J. R. Mantey argued that heaven decides first and the church on earth only declares it (so the NASB, "shall have been bound"). H. J. Cadbury replied that the form is an ordinary future. Stanley Porter and others stress its sense of a settled state. The Plain English Translation's "will stand bound" keeps that sense and leaves both readings open. In 16:19 the words go to Peter alone ("you" singular); in 18:18 to the disciples ("you" plural). Compare John 20:23 on forgiving and retaining sins.
orig: ὃ ἐὰν δήσῃς ... ἔσται δεδεμένον (ho ean dēsēs ... estai dedemenon)

a: they were to tell no one that he was the Messiah
p: "Messiah" meant a king to many Jews. Jesus first had to teach what kind of Messiah he was.
b: Jesus orders silence after the confession, as after healings (8:4; 9:30; 12:16). For many Jews of the time, "Messiah" meant a son of David who would drive out the Romans; announcing one in Galilee could start a revolt and bring Rome's swords. Jesus immediately begins to teach that the Messiah must suffer (16:21). William Wrede (1901) argued that the "messianic secret" was a device of Mark's to explain why Jesus was not recognized; most scholars today think it has some basis in Jesus' own caution.

a: From then on Jesus began to make clear to his disciples what had to happen.
t: A turning point in the story
p: "From then on Jesus began" repeats 4:17. Some scholars divide Matthew at these two points.
b: The same words open Jesus' preaching in 4:17: "From then on Jesus began to preach." Jack Dean Kingsbury argued that these two lines divide Matthew into three parts: who Jesus is (1:1–4:16), his preaching to Israel (4:17–16:20), and his road to the cross (16:21–28:20). Others follow B. W. Bacon in building the book around the five discourses, each ending "When Jesus had finished" (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Both patterns may be present. Either way, from here on Jesus speaks openly of his death, three times on the way to Jerusalem (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:17–19). "Had to" (dei) points to God's plan written in Scripture (26:54).

a: on the third day he would be raised
p: The phrase is old church confession (1 Corinthians 15:4) and may echo Hosea 6:2.
b: Paul hands on the early creed that Christ "has been raised on the third day, in line with the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:4). The Scripture most often suggested is Hosea 6:2, where Israel says God "will raise us up on the third day," and Jesus himself points to Jonah's three days in the fish (12:40). "Be raised" is passive: God raises him. Matthew uses the phrase in all three predictions (16:21; 17:23; 20:19).

a: Heaven spare you, Lord!
p: The Greek idiom means "May God be merciful to you," that is, "God forbid!"
b: Hileōs soi is short for "(May God be) merciful to you," an idiom for "Far from it!" The Greek Old Testament uses it for Hebrew chalilah, "far be it" (2 Samuel 20:20; 1 Chronicles 11:19). Peter, just praised, now "rebukes" Jesus, the word used for silencing demons and storms (8:26; 17:18). He cannot fit a suffering Messiah into what "Messiah" means to him.

a: Go, get behind me, Satan!
t: Back to his place behind Jesus
p: The words echo Jesus' answer to the devil in the wilderness. "Behind me" also tells Peter where a disciple belongs.
b: "Go, Satan!" are Jesus' words to the devil in 4:10, when the devil offered him the world's kingdoms without the cross. Peter, without knowing it, makes the same offer. "Satan" means "adversary," and Jesus treats the suggestion as the devil's. But Jesus adds "behind me" (opisō mou), the same words he uses next: "Anyone who wishes to come behind me" (16:24). Peter is not driven away; he is sent back to his place as a follower. The rock of 16:18 has become a skandalon, a stone to trip over in Jesus' path (compare Isaiah 8:14).
orig: Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ (hypage opisō mou, Satana)

a: pick up his cross
p: Before Easter, these words pictured a condemned man carrying his crossbeam to execution.
b: Rome crucified rebels and slaves, and the condemned man carried the crossbeam to the place of death (27:32). Galileans knew the sight: after a revolt in 4 BC the Roman general Varus crucified two thousand Jews (Josephus, Jewish War 2.75). To "pick up his cross" meant to walk as someone already condemned, ready to lose everything. Christians since the early church have also read it of daily self-denial (Luke 9:23 adds "daily"). Jesus said much the same when he sent out the Twelve (10:38–39).

a: Anyone set on saving his life will lose it.
p: One Greek word means both "life" and "soul." Jesus plays on both senses.
b: Psychē is a person's life, the self, what older English called the soul. In 16:25–26 Jesus uses it four times. Clinging to your life in this world loses the true life; losing it for Jesus finds it. The KJV renders it "life" in 16:25 and "soul" in 16:26, which hides the link. The Plain English Translation keeps "life" throughout. In the Bible the psychē is not a part of a person that floats free of the body, but the whole living person, which God can give back (10:28 speaks of the whole person before God).

a: he will pay back each one for the way he has acted
t: Paid back for what he has done
p: A line from the Psalms and Proverbs, applied to the Son of Man as judge.
b: The Psalms say of God, "you pay each person back by what he does" (Psalm 62:12), and Proverbs says God "will give every human being what his deeds deserve" (Proverbs 24:12). Here the Son of Man does God's work as judge, coming "with his angels" as in Zechariah 14:5 and Daniel 7:10. Matthew develops the scene in 25:31–46. Christians agree on judgment by deeds; they differ on how it fits with salvation by grace (Romans 2:6; Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:24).
r: Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Zechariah 14:5; Daniel 7:10–14; 25:31–46; Romans 2:6; Revelation 22:12

a: some who will never taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom
p: One of the hardest promises in the Gospels. Did it come true, and when?
b: "Taste death" means die. Readings: The transfiguration, which comes next: three disciples see Jesus in glory (most of the fathers, including Chrysostom; 2 Peter 1:16–18 calls it his "majesty"). The resurrection and Jesus' claim to all authority (28:18), with Pentecost. The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, seen as the Son of Man's judgment (preterist readers). The Second Coming, which Jesus expected within a generation; many critical scholars since Albert Schweitzer think he was mistaken, and that early Christians wrestled with the delay (2 Peter 3:4–9). Matthew sets the promise right before the transfiguration, which suggests he saw at least a foretaste there.

a: Six days later
p: Six days, a cloud, a voice, a shining face, three companions: the scene recalls Moses on Sinai.
b: At Sinai "the cloud covered it six days. On the seventh day he called to Moses out of the middle of the cloud" (Exodus 24:16). Moses went up with three named men, Aaron, Nadab and Abihu (Exodus 24:1, 9), and came down with a shining face (Exodus 34:29–30). Here Jesus goes up with three, his face shines, a bright cloud covers them and a voice speaks from it. Dale Allison and others have shown how much Matthew presents Jesus as a new Moses; the voice's "Listen to him" (17:5) points to the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15).
r: Exodus 24:1; Exodus 24:9; Exodus 24:15–18; Exodus 34:29–35; Deuteronomy 18:15; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36

a: a high mountain
p: The Gospels do not say. Tradition names Mount Tabor; many modern scholars prefer Mount Hermon.
b: Since the 300s Christians have pointed to Mount Tabor, a rounded hill rising from the Jezreel valley in lower Galilee (Cyril of Jerusalem, Jerome), and churches have stood on it since the Byzantine era. Against it: Tabor is not very high (about 1,900 feet), and a village and fort may have stood on top in Jesus' time. Many modern scholars prefer Mount Hermon (over 9,000 feet), near Caesarea Philippi, where the previous scene took place (16:13). Others suggest Mount Meron. Matthew seems more interested in what the mountain means than in where it was.

a: he was transformed
p: The Greek verb gives English "metamorphosis." Paul uses it for believers being changed.
b: Metamorphoō means to change form. The Latin Bible's transfiguratus est gave English "transfigured." Jesus' outward form shows a glory that belongs to him: Matthew adds to Mark that "his face blazed like the sun," as the righteous will "blaze like the sun" in the kingdom (13:43; Daniel 12:3). Paul uses the same verb for believers "being transformed" into the Lord's image (2 Corinthians 3:18; Romans 12:2). Orthodox Christians see in the Taboric light the uncreated glory of God, which the saints can share (the teaching of Gregory Palamas). The church keeps the feast of the Transfiguration on 6 August.
r: 13:43; Daniel 12:3; Daniel 10:6; 2 Corinthians 3:18; Romans 12:2; Revelation 1:16; Mark 9:2–3

a: Moses and Elijah
p: The Law and the Prophets, two men who met God on a mountain and whose deaths were mysterious.
b: Moses gave the Law; Elijah was the first great prophet. Both met God on Sinai, also called Horeb (Exodus 24; Exodus 33:18–23; 1 Kings 19:8–18). Both left this life in an unusual way: no one knows where Moses was buried (Deuteronomy 34:6), and Elijah "went up to the heavens in the windstorm" (2 Kings 2:11). The last words of the prophets name them together (Malachi 4:4–5). Readers have taken them as the Law and the Prophets bearing witness to Jesus (5:17; Luke 24:27), and as forerunners of the end time. Luke 9:31 adds that they spoke of his "departure" in Jerusalem.
r: Malachi 4:4–5; Deuteronomy 34:6; 2 Kings 2:11; 1 Kings 19:8–18; 5:17; Luke 9:30–31; Revelation 11:3–6

a: three booths
p: Peter wants to build booths like those of the Feast of Booths. He wants to make the moment last.
b: Skēnē is a tent or booth, the word for the huts of the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:42–43) and for the tabernacle, God's tent among his people. Some scholars think the scene took place near the feast, when Jews lived in booths and hoped for God's final kingdom (Zechariah 14:16–19). Peter may want to house the heavenly visitors and keep the glory on the mountain. Mark 9:6 says he did not know what to say; Matthew is kinder, and has Peter ask "if you want." The answer comes from the cloud: not three booths for three equals, but one Son to listen to.

a: a cloud full of light cast its shadow over them
p: The bright cloud is the cloud of glory that filled the tabernacle.
b: God's presence came in a cloud at the exodus and at Sinai. "The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34), and the Greek of Exodus 40:35 uses the same verb, "overshadow," as here. Later Jewish writers called this presence the Shekhinah. Luke uses the verb again when the Spirit "overshadows" Mary (Luke 1:35). A cloud full of light is Matthew's own touch: God's glory without darkness.
r: Exodus 40:34–35; Exodus 24:15–18; 1 Kings 8:10–11; Luke 1:35; Acts 1:9; Daniel 7:13

a: This is my dearly loved Son; in him I take delight. Listen to him!
p: The words of the baptism, plus Moses' "You must listen to him."
b: The voice repeats the words of 3:17, which join Psalm 2:7 (the king as God's son), Isaiah 42:1 (the servant in whom God delights) and perhaps Genesis 22:2 (Abraham's "only one, whom you love"). Now it adds "Listen to him!", from Moses' promise of a prophet like himself: "You must listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15). The Law and the Prophets have appeared; the voice points away from them to the Son. 2 Peter 1:17–18 recalls the voice as the apostles' own witness.
r: 3:17; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Genesis 22:2; Deuteronomy 18:15; 2 Peter 1:17–18; Acts 3:22–23

a: the vision
p: Only Matthew calls it a vision. The word does not mean it was imaginary.
b: Horama means something seen. In the New Testament it is used of real sights given by God, such as Moses' burning bush (Acts 7:31) and Peter's rescue, which he at first thought was a vision (Acts 12:9). Readings: A historical event seen by three disciples, as the church has held and 2 Peter 1:16–18 claims. A visionary experience given to the disciples, real but seen in a vision (some modern scholars). A resurrection appearance moved back into Jesus' lifetime (Rudolf Bultmann and others); most scholars now reject this, since the scene has none of the marks of the Easter stories. The command to silence links the vision with the resurrection: only after Easter will it make sense.

a: Then why do the scribes say Elijah has to come first?
p: Malachi promised that Elijah would come before the day of the Lord. Jewish hope still waits for him.
b: Malachi ends: God will send Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD, to turn the hearts of parents and children toward each other (Malachi 4:5–6). Sirach 48:10 says he will "restore the tribes of Jacob." The Mishnah has Elijah settle disputes and bring peace when he comes (Mishnah Eduyot 8:7), and Justin Martyr reports a Jew's view that the Messiah would be unknown until Elijah anointed him (Dialogue with Trypho 8). Jewish families still open the door for Elijah at the Passover meal. The disciples ask: if Jesus is the Messiah, where was Elijah?

a: Elijah came already
p: Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the promised Elijah. John's Gospel has John deny it.
b: Jesus already said of John, "John himself is Elijah, the one who was going to come" (11:14), and John dressed like Elijah (3:4; 2 Kings 1:8). In John 1:21 the Baptist says he is not Elijah, and Luke says he would "walk ahead of the Lord with Elijah's spirit and power" (Luke 1:17), which shows how the two statements were reconciled: John fulfilled Elijah's role, not his person. Jesus says Elijah "is coming" and also "came already," which some Christians read as two comings: John before Jesus' first coming, and Elijah himself before the end (Augustine; compare Revelation 11:3–6). Jewish readers have never accepted John as Elijah.

a: He is moonstruck
p: The Greek word blames the moon. The signs match epilepsy. The text also speaks of a demon.
b: Selēniazetai means "is moonstruck" (KJV "lunatick"), from selēnē, the moon. Ancient people often blamed the moon for seizures, and the falling into fire and water fit epilepsy, as most modern translations recognize. Matthew also says a demon came out (17:18), as Mark 9:17–27 describes at length. Readers differ on how to hold the two: some take the demon literally and the epilepsy as its symptom; others see the ancient explanation of an illness now known to be medical. The difference matters: epilepsy is not demon possession, and treating people with epilepsy as possessed has caused real harm.

a: Oh, faithless and warped generation!
p: Jesus uses Moses' words, "a warped and twisted generation," and like Moses comes down a mountain to find failure.
b: Moses' song calls Israel "a warped and twisted generation" (Deuteronomy 32:5) and "children with no faithfulness in them" (Deuteronomy 32:20). Like Moses coming down Sinai to find the golden calf (Exodus 32:15–20), Jesus comes down from the mountain of glory to find unbelief and failure below. "How long must I endure you?" sounds like God's complaint in the wilderness (Numbers 14:11, 27). The rebuke may be aimed at the crowd, the disciples or the whole generation; the disciples' failure (17:16, 19–20) is clearly part of it.
r: Deuteronomy 32:5; Deuteronomy 32:20; Exodus 32:15–20; Numbers 14:11; Numbers 14:27; Philippians 2:15; Mark 9:19

a: the size of a mustard seed
p: The tiniest seed and the biggest obstacle: a proverb for doing the impossible.
b: The mustard seed was the proverbial smallest seed (13:31–32). "Moving mountains" was a way of saying "doing the impossible"; the Talmud calls a brilliant teacher an "uprooter of mountains" (Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 64a). Jesus does not say great faith is needed. Even the smallest real faith, trust in God rather than in oneself, can do what seems impossible, because God does it. He repeats the saying after cursing the fig tree (21:21), and Paul knows it too (1 Corinthians 13:2). Readers differ on how literally to take "nothing will be impossible": most see it as a promise about God's power, not a guarantee of whatever the believer wants.

a: handed over into human hands
p: The verb means both "betray" and "hand over." Judas, the leaders, Pilate, and God himself all "hand over" Jesus.
b: Paradidōmi is the key verb of the passion. Judas "hands over" Jesus (10:4; 26:15–16), the leaders hand him to Pilate (27:2, 18), and Pilate hands him over to be crucified (27:26). Behind them stands God's plan: in the Greek of Isaiah 53:6, 12 the servant is "handed over" for sins, and Paul says God "handed him over for us all" (Romans 8:32). There is a sad pun as well: the Son of Man is handed into the hands of the sons of men.
orig: παραδίδοσθαι εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων (paradidosthai eis cheiras anthrōpōn)

a: the men who collected the double drachma
p: A yearly half-shekel paid by Jewish men for the Temple, based on Exodus 30. After AD 70 Rome took it for Jupiter.
b: The law asked every man who was counted in the census to give "half a shekel, by the holy place's shekel" (Exodus 30:13) as an offering. By Jesus' time this had become a yearly tax of two drachmas, collected from Jewish men everywhere for the Temple's daily sacrifices. The Mishnah says collectors set up tables in the towns in the month of Adar (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3). Not all agreed on it: priests claimed to be exempt, and a text from Qumran (4Q159, the Ordinances) says it should be paid only once in a lifetime. After the Temple was destroyed in AD 70, Rome made Jews pay the same amount to the temple of Jupiter in Rome (Josephus, Jewish War 7.218). Some scholars think Matthew's readers would have heard the story as advice about that humiliating tax.

a: So the sons go free.
p: Kings do not tax their own sons. Jesus and his disciples are God's sons, yet they pay to avoid giving offense.
b: Jesus argues from the way kings behave: royal families do not pay the king's taxes. If the Temple tax is paid to God, God's own children should be free of it. "The sons" is plural: Jesus includes his disciples as God's children. Still he pays, "so that we do not trip them up." Readings: Jesus and the Temple: as the Son, he is greater than the Temple (12:6), yet he honors it. A principle of freedom and love: believers give up rights rather than become a stumbling block, as Paul teaches (1 Corinthians 9:19; Romans 14:13–21). Taxes after AD 70: Matthew's readers should pay the tax Rome now demanded rather than provoke trouble (compare 22:21).

a: a stater
p: A stater was a silver four-drachma coin, enough for two people's tax. The Temple valued the shekel of Tyre.
b: The stater, or tetradrachm, was worth four drachmas: exactly the tax for Jesus and Peter. The Temple valued the shekel of Tyre, a heavy silver coin of reliable purity, even though it bore the image of the god Melqart. Rabbinic texts say that the "silver" of the Torah means Tyrian silver (Mishnah Bekhorot 8:7; Tosefta Ketubot 13:20 in Zuckermandel's numbering). A fish that has swallowed a shiny object is not impossible; the tilapia of the lake is still sold as "St. Peter's fish." Matthew does not tell us that Peter went fishing or found the coin. Most readers take it as a miracle that follows Jesus' word. Others read it as a figure of speech ("go and earn it with a catch"), or as a legend. The story's point lies in 17:25–27a: the sons are free, but love pays.

a: So who ranks highest in the kingdom of heaven?
p: Ancient groups cared about rank. The Dead Sea community listed members in order every year.
b: The disciples' question was natural in their world, where honor and seating order mattered (20:20–28; 23:6–7; Luke 14:7–11). The community of the Dead Sea Scrolls ranked its members each year and made them sit and speak in that order (Community Rule, 1QS 2:19–23; 5:23–24; 6:8–10). In Mark 9:33–34 the disciples argue about it on the road. Matthew turns the question into the start of a discourse on how a community of Jesus should live together.

a: turn around and become like the little children
p: Children in the ancient world had no status or rights. Becoming like them means accepting lowliness.
b: Ancient writers did not idealize children as innocent. A child was a person without power or standing, under others' authority. "Turn around" (strephō) is close to the word for repentance. Readings: Humility: the next verse explains, "anyone who makes himself low like this child" (18:4), the view of most commentators. Trust and dependence on the Father, like a child's. Innocence, a reading popular since the 1800s but less likely in Matthew's world. The demand reverses the disciples' question: the way up is down.
orig: στραφῆτε καὶ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία (straphēte kai genēsthe hōs ta paidia)

a: takes in one child like this for my name's sake
p: In the Roman world unwanted babies were often abandoned. Jews and Christians refused the practice.
b: Roman law let a father reject a newborn, and babies were exposed on rubbish heaps, especially girls and the disabled. Jews were known for refusing to expose infants, and the early Christian manual the Didache forbids killing a child "by abortion or after birth" (Didache 2:2). Jesus says more: to receive a child in his name is to receive him (compare 10:40–42; 25:40). "Child" here may also mean a lowly believer, as "little ones" does in 18:6.

a: these little ones who believe in me
p: Children, or humble believers? "Who believe in me" suggests disciples of low standing.
b: "Little ones" (mikroi) runs through the chapter (18:6, 10, 14) and appears in 10:42, where it means disciples. Most scholars think Matthew means believers who are weak, new or of low status, whose faith can easily be wrecked. Others take it of children as well, since a child stands in the middle of the group (18:2). Either way, the warning is aimed at the strong: those who "trip up" the weak face a fate worse than drowning. The "donkey's millstone" was the large upper stone of a mill turned by an animal, too heavy for any swimmer. Drowning was a known punishment: Josephus tells of Galileans who drowned Herod's supporters in the lake (Antiquities 14.450).

a: Woe to the world because of its snares!
p: A skandalon was the trigger of a trap, then anything that makes someone fall.
b: Skandalon first meant the stick that springs a trap; then any snare or stone that trips someone, and so anything that leads a person to fall away from God. The verb skandalizō means to trip someone up (18:6, 8–9), and also to take offense (13:57; 15:12). Matthew uses the family of words more than any other Gospel (13:41; 16:23; 17:27; 24:10; 26:31–33). "Snares have to come": in a fallen world they are certain, but that does not excuse the one who sets them.

a: cut it off and fling it away from you
p: Jesus said this in 5:29–30 about lust. Here it may also apply to the community.
b: The saying repeats 5:29–30 in a new setting. Nearly all Christian teachers have read it as hyperbole, a vivid way to say "remove whatever leads you to sin, at any cost," not a command to maim the body. Eusebius reports that the young Origen castrated himself, taking another saying (19:12) literally; the church later forbade self-mutilation. In this chapter about the community, some scholars, ancient and modern, read hand, foot and eye as members of the church who lead others astray, a link with the discipline of 18:15–17 and Paul's "body" language (1 Corinthians 12:12–27).

a: the fire of Gehenna
p: Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom, named, not translated. See the note at 5:22.
b: Geenna is the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children had been burned to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31) and which became a Jewish name for the place of final punishment. English "hell" hides the place name. See the full note at 5:22. Here "the fire of Gehenna" stands beside "the eternal fire" of 18:8. Christians differ on whether the fire means endless conscious punishment, final destruction, or purifying judgment; Matthew develops the theme in 25:41, 46.
orig: τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρός (tēn geennan tou pyros)

a: their angels in heaven are always looking on the face of my Father
p: The little ones have angels who stand before God, like a king's closest servants.
b: Jews in Jesus' time believed that angels watched over people and nations: "he will give his angels orders about you" (Psalm 91:11), Raphael guards Tobias in the book of Tobit, and the disciples in Acts 12:15 say, "It is his angel." To "see the face" of a king meant to be one of his closest advisers, like the Persian officials who "had the right to see the king face to face" (Esther 1:14). So the least important believers have advocates in God's inner circle. This verse is the main New Testament basis for belief in guardian angels; churches differ on how far to take it (see the card on the chapter page).
r: Psalm 91:11; Psalm 34:7; Acts 12:15; Hebrews 1:14; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20–21; Esther 1:14; Tobit 5:4

a: leave the ninety-nine on the hillsides
t: The straying sheep: Matthew and Luke
p: Luke tells this parable to Pharisees about sinners. Matthew tells it to disciples about straying believers.
b: In Luke 15:4–7 Jesus answers Pharisees who complain that he eats with sinners, and the sheep is "lost." In Matthew Jesus speaks to his disciples about "little ones" in the community, and the sheep "strays" (planaō, the word for being led astray). Matthew's shepherd "manages to find it" only perhaps (18:13), so the search has no guarantee. The image comes from Ezekiel 34, where God condemns shepherds who do not look for the strays and promises to search for them himself (Ezekiel 34:4–16). The Gospel of Thomas (107) has a later version in which the stray is the largest sheep, loved most.

a: go and correct him, with just the two of you there
p: Leviticus commands loving correction. The Dead Sea Scrolls lay down the same steps Jesus gives.
b: Leviticus says, "Do not hate your brother in your heart. Be sure to correct your fellow citizen, so that you do not carry sin because of him" (Leviticus 19:17). The Dead Sea community turned this into a procedure: a member must rebuke another "in truth, humility and loving kindness" on the same day, and may not bring a matter before the assembly without first rebuking him before witnesses (Community Rule, 1QS 5:24–6:1; Damascus Document 9:2–8). Jesus' steps are similar: privately, then with witnesses, then before the community. The goal is stated first: "you have won your brother back."

a: every statement may stand on the word of two or three witnesses
p: The rule of witnesses from Deuteronomy, used here first to persuade and then to confirm.
b: Deuteronomy says, "A matter is to stand on the word of two witnesses or on the word of three witnesses" (Deuteronomy 19:15), a protection against false accusation in court. Jesus applies it inside the community. The witnesses may help the brother see his fault, and if he still refuses, they can confirm what happened. Paul uses the same rule (2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:19).
r: Deuteronomy 19:15; Deuteronomy 17:6; 2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:19; Hebrews 10:28; John 8:17

a: regard him as you regard the Gentile and the tax collector
t: Like a Gentile and a tax collector
p: It sounds like exclusion. Yet Jesus welcomed tax collectors and Gentiles. What does it mean?
b: Spoken in a Jewish setting, "the Gentile and the tax collector" were people outside the covenant community, with whom an observant Jew did not share meals. Exclusion: most interpreters read it as removing the unrepentant member from fellowship, as Paul commands (1 Corinthians 5:11–13); this is the root of excommunication and the ban. Exclusion for the sake of return: Paul also says, "do not treat him like an enemy. Correct him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15), and the next parable is about forgiveness (18:21–35). Treat him as Jesus treated such people: some point out that Jesus ate with tax collectors and welcomed Gentiles (9:10–13; 8:5–13), so the outsider becomes someone to win again. Matthew himself was a tax collector (9:9; 10:3). "The church" here is the local gathering of believers; see the note at 16:18.

a: anything you bind on earth will stand bound in heaven
p: The words given to Peter in 16:19 are now given to the community: "you" is plural.
b: In 16:19 the binding and loosing are given to Peter; here the "you" is plural, spoken to the disciples who are asking about life in the community (18:1). In context the words concern the decision of 18:17: the church's verdict about a sinning member stands before God. John 20:23 gives the same power in terms of sins: "If you forgive anyone their sins, those sins have been forgiven them." Churches understand this power differently: as the priest's absolution, the preaching of the gospel, or the whole congregation's discipline (see the cards on this page and at 16:19).

a: if two of you here on earth are of one mind about any matter they ask for
t: A promise about prayer, or about judgment?
p: Often quoted as a promise for any prayer. In context it is about deciding a case in the church.
b: Taken alone, this verse promises that the Father will do whatever two believers agree to ask. Some churches teach a "prayer of agreement" on that basis. In context, though, "two" and "three" pick up the witnesses of 18:16, and "any matter" (pragma) can mean a legal case (1 Corinthians 6:1). Many commentators therefore read 18:19–20 as a promise that God stands behind the community's decision when it seeks his will together. The two readings need not exclude each other, but the setting of church discipline should not be lost.

a: I am right there in the middle of them
p: A rabbinic saying puts God's presence between two who study Torah. Here Jesus himself is present.
b: The Mishnah records a teaching of Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion: when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Divine Presence (Shekhinah) rests between them (Mishnah Avot 3:2; compare 3:6). Jesus' promise has the same shape, but now he is the presence. Matthew frames his Gospel with this idea: Jesus is "Immanuel, God with us" (1:23), and he promises, "I myself am with you every day" (28:20). For many Jewish readers, the saying shows how fully Matthew puts Jesus in the place of God's presence; for Christians it grounds the confidence that Christ is present in the gathered church, however small.

a: how many times do I forgive him? Up to seven times?
p: Later rabbis said to forgive a repeated wrong three times. Peter's seven is generous.
b: A teaching in the Talmud says that a person who wrongs another is forgiven a first, second and third time, but not a fourth (Babylonian Talmud Yoma 86b, building on Amos 1–2). That rule is later than Jesus, but it shows Peter's "seven times" as a generous offer, the number of completeness. Luke 17:4 has "seven times in one day." Jewish teaching also stresses that the one who wronged must ask forgiveness and make it right; Matthew's parable focuses on the duty of the one who has been forgiven.

a: up to seventy-seven times
p: The Greek can mean either. It is the exact phrase of Lamech's song in the Greek of Genesis 4:24.
b: Hebdomēkontakis hepta can mean "seventy-seven times" or "seventy times seven" (490), the KJV's choice. The Greek of Genesis 4:24 uses the same words for Lamech's boast of revenge: "Cain will be avenged sevenfold, but Lamech seventy and seven" (Genesis 4:24). That makes "seventy-seven" likely, and it makes the point clear: the endless vengeance that began with Lamech is reversed by endless forgiveness. Either number means "without counting."

a: a human king
t: "A human king": a Jewish parable form
p: "A man, a king" is how rabbis began many parables: "to a king of flesh and blood."
b: The Greek anthrōpō basilei, "a man, a king," sounds odd, but it matches a common opening of rabbinic parables: "A parable: to what may this be compared? To a king of flesh and blood who..." The earthly king stands for God, and the story about him shows what God is like. Matthew uses the same opening in 22:2. The rabbinic parables are written down later than the Gospels, but they show that Jesus taught in a Jewish form his hearers knew.

a: ten thousand talents
p: Ten thousand was the largest Greek number, and the talent the largest unit of money: a debt beyond imagining.
b: A talent was about 6,000 denarii, and a denarius was a day's wage for a laborer (20:2). Ten thousand talents would be some sixty million days' wages. For comparison, Josephus says Herod Antipas took in two hundred talents a year from all of Galilee and Perea (Antiquities 17.318). Ten thousand (myrioi) was the biggest number Greek had a word for. The slave could never pay. The point is the size of what God forgives.

a: gave orders to sell him, and his wife and children
p: Debt slavery was common in the ancient world. The scene suggests a Gentile king's court.
b: Ancient creditors could sell a debtor and his family into slavery. Israel's law allowed debt service but limited it and freed the servant in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2–4; Leviticus 25:39–41). Elisha met a widow whose creditor was coming "to take my two boys for himself as slaves" (2 Kings 4:1). Selling a wife and handing a debtor over to torturers (18:34) were not allowed under Jewish law, which suggests the parable pictures a Gentile king, perhaps like the Hellenistic rulers whose officials farmed taxes and owed huge sums. The sale would cover only a tiny part of the debt; it is punishment, not repayment.

a: a hundred denarii
p: About a hundred days' wages: a real debt, but one that could be paid.
b: A hundred denarii was about a third of a year's wages, a serious sum but payable. Set beside ten thousand talents, it is about one six-hundred-thousandth. The fellow slave uses the very words the first slave used (18:26, 29), and gets the opposite answer. The listener sees the injustice at once, and so is trapped into judging himself, as Nathan trapped David (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

a: handed him over to the torturers
p: Torture of debtors to find hidden money was known in the ancient world. What does it say about God?
b: Basanistai are torturers or harsh jailers. Debtors were sometimes tortured to make them reveal hidden wealth or to push their families to pay. Since the debt could never be paid, the sentence has no end. Readers ask how far the picture applies to God. Most say the point is the seriousness of refusing mercy, as 18:35 states, not a description of hell's details. Some Catholic writers have linked "until he paid" (compare 5:25–26) with purgatory, a temporary purification; most commentators, Catholic included, read this parable of final judgment. Others stress that Jesus uses a shocking, worldly king to make a point by contrast.

a: My heavenly Father will do the same to you
t: Does God's forgiveness depend on ours?
p: The master forgave first. But the parable ends with the forgiveness taken back.
b: This verse repeats the warning after the Lord's Prayer (6:14–15). Readers hold together two sides. Grace comes first: the master forgave freely, before the slave did anything; forgiving others is a response to mercy received, not a way to earn it. The warning is real: a person who refuses to forgive shows that he has not truly received mercy, and so loses it. Catholic teaching speaks of grace that can be lost by grave sin; Reformed teaching that true faith always bears this fruit, so the unforgiving slave shows a faith that was never real; Wesleyan teaching that a believer can fall from grace. All agree on the practical point: forgiveness must come "from the heart," not only in words.
